subtype: Approach: trying to relearn everything from scratch [Pitfall]
passage: Devika opened her history book to Chapter 1 on the first evening of the last month before the board exams, then did the same with science, maths and civics. "Basics first," she told herself, and copied out the early chapters in neat handwriting. On Friday in the school library, Sahil saw three books open to early chapters. "Isn't it week three?" he asked. She checked her planner. History had reached Chapter 8 of 15, maths Chapter 7 of 14, and she had not touched the last chapters of any book. "Those carry the most marks," Sahil said quietly, holding his own list of high-mark chapters. Devika counted the days left: nine. Her stomach dropped, and the bell rang before she could answer.

qa.q: Which chapter of history had Devika reached by week three?
qa.a: History had reached Chapter 8 of 15.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she counted the days left?
qa.a: Devika felt alarmed and dismayed; her stomach dropped when she saw how much of the syllabus was still untouched. 😰

qa.q: What different approach could Devika use for the last nine days, and why would it help?
qa.a: She could rank chapters by marks and do the heavily weighted last chapters first, revising earlier ones only where she has gaps, because time is short and those chapters carry the most marks.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Devika's plan?
qa.a: Sahil sees a hardworking classmate spending scarce days at the wrong end of the books, so he gently points out the high-mark chapters from his own list.

grounding: The student restarts every book from Chapter 1, finishes only about half the syllabus by week three, and leaves the heavily weighted final chapters untouched.

subtype: Approach: active recall with mock tests [Action]
passage:
Tanuja: Paper three is done. Two hours, timed.
Elizabeth: Third one this week?
Tanuja: Monday, Wednesday, today. Every other day. Pass me the marking scheme.
Elizabeth: Why not just reread your notes? They feel nicer.
Tanuja: Nicer, yes. Look: 31 out of 40 in algebra, 14 out of 40 in mensuration. Again. My notes made me feel finished with both.
Elizabeth: Ouch. So what now?
Tanuja: Tonight is only mensuration, and the questions I lost marks on. Friday I write the next paper.
Elizabeth: Can I borrow the paper? I'll sit at the next desk and time myself.
Tanuja: Start when I say. Phones face down.
Elizabeth: Fine 🙂 but snacks after.

qa.q: How often does Tanuja write a timed paper?
qa.a: Every other day: Monday, Wednesday and today, that week.

qa.q: What does Tanuja think about rereading notes compared with the paper scores?
qa.a: Tanuja feels wary of the comfort of notes, since they made mensuration seem finished when the score of 14 out of 40 said otherwise.

qa.q: What other approach could Tanuja add alongside the mock papers, and why?
qa.a: Writing a one-page summary of each weak topic after marking would help, because choosing what matters in mensuration turns the score into targeted revision.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Tanuja's routine at first?
qa.a: Elizabeth doubts it and asks why not reread notes, but the scores persuade Elizabeth enough to ask for the paper and time a session too.

grounding: Every alternate day the student writes a timed paper and checks it against the marking scheme, so scores show which topics slip and revision becomes targeted.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem before the plan starts [Thinking]
passage: On the veranda of her family's farmhouse, Shalini wrote a line at the top of a fresh page: exam day, and under it, "I failed because..." Then she made herself keep going. Phone, she wrote, since the videos on Uncle's handset never stop. A sick week, because monsoon fevers go through the village every year. Skipped sleep, from the night-before panic. Chandrika, the neighbour, leaned over the wall with a guava. "What is this, a funeral notice?" "A plan," said Shalini. Beside each reason she added a step: phone in the cupboard until six, three chapters photocopied at the shop in town in case of fever, lights out by ten. Chandrika read it and reached for a pen. "Now it can't surprise me," Shalini said.

qa.q: What reasons for failure did Shalini list?
qa.a: Phone, a sick week and skipped sleep.

qa.q: What does Shalini's line 'Now it can't surprise me' suggest about how Shalini feels?
qa.a: Shalini feels calmer and more in control, because each fear now has a protective step beside it. 🙂

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shalini add beyond the list, and why?
qa.a: A weekly mock paper marked against the answers would show which chapters slip, while the list only guards against risks Shalini has already predicted.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see the page of failure reasons?
qa.a: Chandrika first finds it gloomy and jokes about a funeral notice, but after reading the steps sees a practical plan and reaches for a pen to make one too.

grounding: The student imagines exam day with revision failed, lists likely causes such as phone, illness and skipped sleep, and adds a protective step for each before the plan begins.

passage:
Monday: Rajni's physics mock came back with 38 out of 100. That night she stayed at her desk until the window turned grey, reading the same three chapters again and again.

Wednesday: Jahnavi found her in the corridor, eyes red, and asked for the formula sheet Rajni had promised. Rajni could not remember where a motion problem even started. "Stop asking me things!" she snapped. She had spent a second night awake.

Friday: In the class test, her mind went blank at question two. Afterwards she counted on her fingers: eleven extra hours gained, and she had forgotten more than she had learned. Jahnavi sat beside her with a bottle of water and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How many marks did Rajni score in the physics mock?
qa.a: Rajni scored 38 out of 100.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when 'Stop asking me things!' came out, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Rajni was frazzled, anxious and short of sleep; the red eyes and forgetting a problem after a night at the desk suggest it.

qa.q: What approach to the last month could work better than all-nighters, and why?
qa.a: A steady schedule with fixed sleep and a mock paper marked for weak topics would work better, because a rested memory holds what was studied.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Rajni's late-night plan?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees a friend worn out and struggling, so Jahnavi offers water and quiet company instead of arguing. 🤍

grounding: Anxiety after a bad mock pushes the student into all-nighters, and two nights of poor sleep cost her memory and mood, erasing the extra hours.

passage:
Saurabh: how many chapters of the physics sheet done
Lalit: 4 out of 11. chapter 5 took 2 hrs 😩
Saurabh: 2 hrs for ONE page??
Lalit: had to pick what actually matters. Ended up with 9 formulas. Before I'd have copied 30
Saurabh: hmm. so that's the point
Lalit: plus one circuit diagram and a unit list. that's it
Saurabh: ok doing chem tonight. printing them so I can read on the bus in the last week
Lalit: 👍 read the sheets daily, not the book
Saurabh: deal. send me your ch5 pic?
Lalit: sending. but make your own, the choosing is half the value

qa.q: How many formulas did Lalit end up with on the chapter 5 sheet?
qa.a: Lalit ended up with 9 formulas.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the two hours spent on the chapter 5 sheet?
qa.a: Lalit was worn out but satisfied; the tired emoji shows the effort, and cutting 30 formulas to 9 shows why it felt worth it.

qa.q: What could Saurabh add to check whether the sheets are working, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could write a timed mock from memory and mark it, because the scores show whether the sheets hold the essentials.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Lalit's advice to make their own sheet?
qa.a: Saurabh probably sees it as fair, having already said "so that's the point" about the choosing, and plans to do chem that night.

grounding: For each chapter the student condenses key formulas and a diagram onto one page to read in the final week, and making the sheet forces choices about what is essential.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for illness or power cuts [Thinking]
passage: Shalini, beta, sit. You think your Nani never had exams? I am Sarita, and when I was sixteen in Nagpur, April meant two things: the light going off every evening and half the class down with fever. So I sat with my chart and thought, something will break, it always does. I had my notes photocopied and kept the printed set in a folder, so a dark room or a heavy head could not take them. And I left Sunday afternoons empty on purpose, one spare slot. My friend Leela laughed at those empty Sundays. In the third week the fever caught me for three days and the lights went twice. My Sunday was free, and I was caught up by evening. Leela came to my door that week, asking for the printed notes, because her house had no light.

qa.q: What did Sarita leave empty on purpose?
qa.a: Sarita left Sunday afternoons empty on purpose, one spare slot.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel about the chance of a disruption before it happened, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sarita felt realistic and prepared rather than panicked; expecting that 'something will break,' Sarita photocopied notes and kept a spare Sunday.

qa.q: Besides printed notes and an empty Sunday, what other approach could protect a student during a sick week, and why?
qa.a: Sarita could have asked a classmate to share the missed lesson notes, because one spare slot cannot cover a long illness by itself.

qa.q: How did Leela's view of the empty Sundays change?
qa.a: Leela first laughed at the empty Sundays, but when Leela's house had no light, Leela came asking for the printed notes and saw why they mattered.

grounding: Knowing summer power cuts and fevers are common, the student keeps printed notes and a spare Sunday slot so one disruption does not derail the schedule.

subtype: Approach: mid-month check and cutting low-yield topics [Revision]
passage: Halfway through the month, Afreen laid her plan beside her progress chart on the study table and counted. Four chapters behind. Her first thought was to sit up later. Instead she pulled out the last six years of papers and marked which topics turned up in every one: probability, matrices, integration. Two chapters had appeared only once. The next day she showed her list to Ojas Sir after class. He read it, tapped one chapter, and said, "Leave these two. But keep this one, it comes as a short question." That evening Afreen crossed out the two chapters, moved their hours to probability and matrices, and rewrote the week. The gap did not vanish, but for the first time the calendar looked possible.

qa.q: How many chapters was Afreen behind at the halfway point?
qa.a: Afreen was four chapters behind.

qa.q: What does the calendar looking possible for the first time suggest about Afreen's mood?
qa.a: Afreen felt relieved and hopeful, because the cuts turned a worrying gap into a plan that fits the days left. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could protect Afreen against a surprise question from a dropped chapter, and why?
qa.a: Afreen could keep one-page summaries of the dropped chapters to skim in the last week, since a short read costs little time.

qa.q: How does Ojas Sir see Afreen's list of cuts?
qa.a: Ojas Sir sees a sensible, evidence-based plan, agrees to two cuts, and flags one chapter to keep because it comes as a short question.

grounding: At the halfway point the student finds she is four chapters behind, drops rarely asked topics with the teacher's agreement, and moves hours to areas that recur in past papers.

subtype: Approach: study group used as social avoidance [Pitfall]
passage: With twelve days left before the pre-board papers, Wasim told his mother he was "studying with the group" every evening. The group met at Bidisha's flat: five phones on the table, a plate of fried snacks in the middle. Books were open. Notes went around. But by seven each evening it was gossip about teachers, an argument about a cricket match and Bidisha's cheese toast. Wasim walked home feeling good. He had been there, hadn't he? Then the chemistry mock came back: 19 out of 50, with questions on chapters the group had "discussed" in name only. He sat in the corridor with the paper, angry at the group and angrier at himself, when Bidisha waved from the stairs. "Same time tomorrow?"

qa.q: Where did the group meet?
qa.a: The group met at Bidisha's flat.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling in the corridor with the chemistry paper?
qa.a: Wasim was angry at the group and angrier at himself, and disappointed to find questions on chapters that were only discussed in name.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Wasim try so the group meetings still help, and why?
qa.a: Each person could quiz the others on one topic for an hour with phones away and snacks only afterwards, since that turns being present into actual recall.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see the evenings?
qa.a: Bidisha likely sees them as friendly, productive time because everyone came and books were open, so Bidisha waves and asks 'Same time tomorrow?' without noticing the problem.

grounding: Meeting friends to study turns into chatting and snacks, feels productive because everyone is present, and the student only realises after a poor mock.

passage: By the second period on Thursday, Pablo knew that half the class had heard about his failed orchestra audition. He had told only Alejandro. His first plan was a furious message listing everything Alejandro had done wrong since primary school. He typed two lines, deleted them and put the phone in his bag. That night at the kitchen table in Valencia, he took a sheet of paper and drew a line down the middle. What hurt: hearing it from Marta first. Feeling laughed at. What I want: for Alejandro to know it hurt, and to be someone I can tell things to again. Pablo read the second column twice. It had never been about winning the argument. On Friday he would ask Alejandro to walk home with him.

qa.q: How many lines did Pablo type before deleting the message?
qa.a: Pablo typed two lines and deleted them.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel about Alejandro telling the class, and where can you tell?
qa.a: Pablo felt hurt and laughed at; the page lists hearing it from Marta first and feeling laughed at.

qa.q: What approach could Pablo take on Friday, and why might it work?
qa.a: Pablo could ask to talk privately and begin with 'I felt hurt when...', because that invites Alejandro to listen without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see the news spreading?
qa.a: Alejandro may not realise how much it hurt, and could feel defensive if blamed, so a calm private request gives Alejandro a chance to listen and repair trust.

grounding: After a friend shares a secret with others, the student waits a night, writes what hurt and what he wants, and realises the goal is to be heard and trusted again, not to win.

passage:
Zeenat: Mehak, can we talk for five minutes? Just us, by the gate.
Mehak: Sure. Is it about the maths thing?
Zeenat: Sort of. When I heard the whole bench knew I still sleep with the hall light on, I felt small. I only told you.
Mehak: I didn't think...
Zeenat: I'm not saying you're a bad friend. I felt really embarrassed, and I want to understand what happened.
Mehak: Ritu asked why you skipped the sleepover and I said too much. I thought it was funny. I'm sorry.
Zeenat: Thanks for telling me. Next time, can you ask me first?
Mehak: Yes. I should have. Want to get chai? 🙂

qa.q: Where did Zeenat ask to talk to Mehak?
qa.a: Zeenat asked to talk just the two of them, by the gate.

qa.q: How does Zeenat feel about the hall light becoming known?
qa.a: Zeenat feels small and embarrassed, because Zeenat only told Mehak.

qa.q: What could Zeenat try if Mehak became defensive, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat could write a short note explaining the hurt and give Mehak time to think, because reading in private can lower defensiveness.

qa.q: How does the conversation look to Mehak?
qa.a: Mehak feels guilty and sorry but not attacked, because Zeenat says 'I felt' and asks what happened instead of accusing.

grounding: The student asks for a one-to-one talk, says how it felt when the secret spread, and asks what happened, naming feelings without accusing.
